# Where the edge actually is {#sec-forward}

Three families of betting rule have now been searched over the settled
starting price and none of them produced a rule that returns a profit at it.
That is the point at which the price, rather than the rule, becomes the thing
to look at.

## Every number in this series is measured at the wrong price

Paper 4 released the constraint that market data stay out of the model and
asked whether the model adds anything *given* a price. Against the settled
starting price it adds nothing distinguishable: the pooled Benter
model-probability coefficient was 0.068 for the paper-2b ranking model and
0.039 for the gradient-boosted trees over 2,182 races, with 95% intervals
reaching no higher than 0.204. Against the overnight racecard forecast price
it adds substantially — 1.037 and 1.026 on the earlier test half, 0.746 and
0.723 on the later.

The model therefore knows something the overnight price does not, and nothing
the settled price does not. Its value sits in the interval between the two,
and **every backtest in papers 1 to 6 is settled at the closing end of that
interval**, which is the one price at which the model is known to add nothing.
Six papers of betting numbers have been optimised against the only price in
the day where the answer was already known to be no.

That reframes what @sec-found found. The searches were not failing to find a
rule; they were searching for a rule good enough to overcome a margin at a
price where the model has no informational advantage left. The margin is not
small:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-margin-forward
p6_tbl(
  p6_overround_val |>
    dplyr::filter(n_races >= 20) |>
    dplyr::transmute(`Field size` = field_size, Races = n_races,
                     `Starting-price margin` = p6_fpct(mean_margin_pct / 100, 1)),
  caption = "What a flat backer pays away at the settled starting price, before any skill enters."
)
```

Field sizes 8 to 12 carry
`r p6_fpct(sum(p6_overround_val$n_races[p6_overround_val$field_size %in% 8:12]) / p6_universe$n_val_races, 0)`
of the search-set races and pay between
`r p6_fpct(min(p6_overround_val$mean_margin_pct[p6_overround_val$field_size %in% 8:12]) / 100, 1)`
and
`r p6_fpct(max(p6_overround_val$mean_margin_pct[p6_overround_val$field_size %in% 8:12]) / 100, 1)`.
Against that, the best test-split return in this paper's whole shortlist is
`r p6_fpct(max(p6_round3_test$roi, na.rm = TRUE), 1, TRUE)`. The fair-book
column says the same thing from the other side: three rules in the shortlist
are profitable with the margin removed, and all three lose with it in place.

## What follows for live betting

Three things, in the order they matter.

**Bet early, into the gap.** The model's demonstrated advantage is over the
overnight price, so the bet has to be struck while some of that gap is still
open. This is the convergence idea the series has carried since paper 4 as a
direction rather than a commitment: early markets are thin and dominated by
bookmaker prices and uninformed money, and they move toward fair value as
race time approaches and liquidity builds. A model that approximates the
closing price using only pre-race information identifies horses whose early
price has not yet converged. The trade is front-running that convergence, not
beating the closing line.

**Judge it by closing line value, not by ROI.** This paper is a
demonstration of why. A 1,505-race window could not rank betting rules at all
(@sec-found), and the intervals on 300-to-1,000-bet samples in @sec-found run
20 to 50 points wide. ROI on a win market converges slowly because almost all
of the variance is in whether a small number of long-priced bets landed —
the field-size rule's whole reversal is 42 winners becoming 19. Closing line
value measures something per bet rather than per win: whether the price taken
was better than the price the market settled at. It is available on every
bet, it does not wait for a result, and it converges in hundreds of bets
rather than tens of thousands. If the early-price thesis is right, closing
line value is positive; if it is wrong, that shows up long before an ROI
would.

**The exchange changes the arithmetic.** The margin in the table above is a
bookmaker over-round baked into the price. An exchange replaces it with
commission on net winnings, in the region of 2 to 5% depending on the account.
That does not create an edge, but it changes what size of edge is needed for
one to survive: a rule losing roughly its margin at the starting price is not
obviously a losing rule at a price struck on an exchange with commission
instead of an over-round.

## Two things this dataset cannot answer

Neither of the following is a caveat in the ordinary sense. They are the two
questions on which the whole forward strategy turns, and this data is silent
on both.

**Is real money available at early prices, in usable size?** Everything above
assumes a bet can be struck at the early price. The Smartform archive records
what prices existed, not what liquidity stood behind them. Early exchange
markets on UK All-Weather handicaps are thin, and a price that exists for one
unit may not exist for fifty. If the available size at the early price is
small enough, the edge is real and unusable, which is operationally the same
as not having it.

**Does the model beat an early *exchange* price?** Paper 4's result is
against `daily_runners.forecast_price_decimal` — a newspaper-style forecast
published the evening before by a compiler, not a price money has traded at.
An early exchange price is a much harder target: it aggregates the opinion of
people who have committed money, and it will already contain much of what a
compiler's forecast misses. Beating a forecast price is weak evidence of
beating an early traded price, and this dataset contains no early traded
prices at all, so the gap cannot be measured here.

**Nothing above asserts that the strategy will work.** It is the direction the
evidence points, and the two questions above are exactly the ones that decide
it. They need a live feed and paper trading, not another backtest on this
archive.

## The place and each-way numbers are against markets that do not quite exist

One correction to the series that this section is the right place for.

Betfair has **no each-way market**. An each-way bet is a bookmaker product:
one stake on the win, one on a place at a fraction of the odds. On an
exchange the two legs are separate markets and the each-way construction has
no counterpart. Every each-way figure in papers 2b, 5 and 6 — at paper 5's
flat one-fifth top-three terms and at the corrected industry ladder alike —
prices a bet that cannot be placed on the venue the forward strategy would
use.

Betfair's place market is a **real, independently priced market**. The place
prices in this series are not: they are a discounted-Harville construction
computed from the win prices, following @harville1973 with the
@lobaconshone1994 corrections. That construction was the right choice for papers 2b to
5, because it makes the place market comparable to the win market on the same
information. It is not the price a place bet would be struck at, and the
difference need not be small — a genuinely traded place market prices the
probability of a top-three finish directly, and can disagree with anything
derived from win prices.

So of the four markets reported throughout this paper, one is real for the
forward strategy (win), one is real but priced here by proxy (place), and two
are products of a venue the strategy would not be using. The win-market
numbers are the ones that carry forward.
